inline.s: Clinging to these four, all manner of discriminations arise.
They reckon Brahmā or Īśvara makes them, one body or many;
or that the sun and moon so move — such a one is no child of mine.
One who is fully possessed of noble vision, who comprehends the Dharma as it really is,
who deftly turns about all his notions, has reached the farther shore of consciousness.
By this seal of liberation he forever leaves behind existence and nonexistence;
and freed from coming and going, such a one is a child of my Dharma.
If form-consciousness were to turn and cease, and the various karmas were to be destroyed,
then there would be no birth and death, and no permanence and no impermanence.
Yet when that turning and ceasing takes place, though the realm of form is cast aside,
karma abides in the ālaya, free from the faults of existence and nonexistence.
Though form-consciousness turns and ceases, karma is not destroyed;
it causes form-consciousness to continue again throughout the various realms of existence.
If the karma produced by those sentient beings were to be destroyed,
then there would be no birth and death, nor would there be nirvāṇa.
If karma and form-consciousness were to perish together at the same time,
then in birth and death, when birth occurs, form and karma would not be distinct.
Form, mind, and discrimination are neither different nor not different;
the foolish speak of their destruction, yet in truth they transcend existence and nonexistence.
Dependent arising and false imagining have no marks distinct from each other;
as with form and impermanence, so too does each arise from the other.
Since they are apart from difference and non-difference, false imagining cannot be known;
like the impermanent nature of form, how can one speak of existence or nonexistence?
One who fully understands false imagining sees that dependent arising does not arise;
by seeing dependent arising, false imagining itself is suchness.
If one destroys the imagined nature, one destroys the eye of Dharma;
and so, within my Dharma, one sets up assertions and slanders it.
People of such a kind will slander the true Dharma;
by what is not Dharma they destroy the eye of my Dharma.
The wise should not speak with them, nor share a monk's affairs;
for by destroying false imagining they establish it and slander it.
If one follows after discrimination and gives rise to views of existence and nonexistence,
such a one is like an illusory hair-net, a dream, a mirage, or a gandharva city.
Such a one does not learn the Buddha's Dharma, and should not be dwelt with;
for he falls into the two extremes himself and ruins others as well.
If there is a practitioner who contemplates the imagined nature,
in stillness apart from existence and nonexistence, one may receive him and dwell with him.
Just as in the world there are places where gold and maṇi gems are found;
though there is no maker there, sentient beings still make use of them.
So too is the nature of karma, far removed from all kinds of natures;
the karma one sees is not existent, yet it is not that the realms are not born.
As the noble ones have understood it, all dharmas are without any own-being;
but the dharmas that the foolish discriminate and falsely imagine are not nonexistent.
If those dharmas that the foolish discriminate were in fact nonexistent,
then since all dharmas are absent, sentient beings would have no defilement.
Yet because there are defiled dharmas, bound by ignorance and craving,
one can give rise to a body of birth and death, with all the faculties complete.
If one says that all these dharmas discriminated by the foolish are nonexistent,
then the faculties would not be born, and that is not right practice.
If these dharmas did not exist as the cause of birth and death,
the foolish, without waiting to practice, would be liberated of themselves.
If those dharmas did not exist, how would the ordinary and the noble differ?
Nor would there be noble ones practicing the three liberations.
The aggregates, the person, and dharmas, in their own and common marks, are markless;
the various conditions and the faculties — these I teach for the śrāvakas.
Mind-only, the non-cause, the stages, and Īśvara;
the inwardly realized, pure suchness — these I teach for the Buddha's children.
In ages yet to come there will be those who wear the kāṣāya robe,
who falsely speak of existence and nonexistence and destroy my true Dharma.
Dependent arising is without own-nature; this is what all the noble ones practice;
the imagined nature is a thing apart, discriminated by those who calculate.
In times to come there will be fools, the Khaṇḍa and other heretics,
who teach the doctrine of no cause, whose wrong views ruin the world.
They falsely declare that all the worlds arise from minute atoms;
and that those atoms have no cause, that the nine kinds of substance are permanent.
From the real comes the real, from the quality is born the quality;
the nature of true Dharma is other than this, yet they slander it and call it nonexistent.
If what was not came to be, the world would then have a beginning;
but birth and death have no beginning — this is what I teach.
If all things in the three realms arose from what was not,
then camels, donkeys, and dogs would grow horns, and of that there could be no doubt.
If eye, form, and consciousness, which were not, now come to be,
then clothes, caps, and mats should be born from a lump of clay.
Just as there is no mat in the reed, and no mat in the bulrush,
why should not a mat be born from each and every one of the conditions?
If the life-principle and the body arise from what was not,
then, as I have said before, all such views are the talk of heretics.
The doctrines I have taught before were set forth to refute their meaning;
and having refuted them, I then teach my own doctrine.
Lest the assembled disciples be deluded and cling to the doctrines of existence and nonexistence,
therefore I first set forth for them the doctrines of the heretics.
Kapila, of evil wisdom, taught his disciples
that the primordial nature gives rise to the world, transformed by the guṇas.
Since the conditions are nonexistent, there is no already-born and no presently-born;
since the conditions are not conditions, there is neither arising nor non-arising.
My doctrine is apart from existence and nonexistence, and apart from all causes and conditions;
arising and ceasing, and the marks they produce, are all entirely left behind.
The world is like an illusion or a dream; causes and conditions are all without own-nature;
always contemplating thus, discrimination never arises again.
If one can regard all that exists as a mirage or a hair-net,
or as a gandharva city, one forever stands apart from existence and nonexistence.
Abandoning causes and conditions altogether, one makes the mind entirely pure;
if one says there is no external object, and that there is only mind.
Without an object there is no mind — how then is mind-only established?
Because there is an object to be perceived, the minds of sentient beings arise.
Without a cause the mind does not arise — how then is mind-only established?
Suchness and mind-only are what all the noble ones practice.
One who says this exists but that does not does not understand my Dharma;
it is from the grasped and the grasper that the mind comes to arise.
The worldly mind is like this, and so it is not mind-only;
body, possessions, land, and images arise from the mind as in a dream.
Though the mind takes on two parts, the mind has no two marks;
as a blade does not cut itself, as a finger does not touch itself.
And the mind does not see itself — so too is this matter;
where there is no image, there is no dependent arising.
The imagined nature too is absent; the five dharmas and the two minds are exhausted;
the producer and the produced are both marks of one's own mind.
It is by hidden intent that the producer is taught, and in truth there is no own-nature;
if the various shapes of objects were born from false imagining,
then space and a rabbit's horn should also become objects;
but since the object arises from the mind, this object is not falsely imagined.
Yet that falsely imagined object cannot be found apart from the mind;
throughout beginningless birth and death, objects are entirely nonexistent.
The mind has no place from which it arises — how then are images formed?
If something could arise from nothing, a rabbit's horn should also arise.
Nothing can arise from nothing, giving rise to discrimination;
just as an object appearing as nonexistent was nonexistent before as well.
How, in a state without objects, could the mind arise toward an object?
Suchness, emptiness, the real limit, nirvāṇa, and the dharma realm —
all dharmas are unborn; this is the nature of the highest meaning.
